name: Urban Suite - Tijuana Bordertowns
catalogPath: Curricular Models/Urban Suite/Urban Suite - Tijuana Bordertowns
miniText: The scientific question is whether migration, income and infrastructure access can jointly shape informal settlement. In NetLogo's Urban Suite - Tijuana Bordertowns model, migrants enter near compatriots, earn and spend money, seek affordable serviced locations and form settlements whose density can trigger infrastructure development. The selected literature connects this mechanism to migration-linked settlement and urban-service inequalities: scholarly border-city studies supply context for Tijuanas distinctive urban conditions [1]; empirical requirements constrain bottom-up residential development modeling [2]; observed urban-expansion research illustrates the need for explicit spatial evidence [3]. The source is a pedagogical design experiment with stylized economic and migration rules; no contemporary Tijuana forecast or calibration is established here. The original NetLogo behavior is the baseline for reimplementation. This simulation offers a controlled thought experiment, and agreement with its output does not establish empirical validation.

modelSource.scientificOrigin: The original version of this model was developed during the Sprawl/Swarm Class at Illinois Institute of Technology in Fall 2006 under the supervision of Sarah Dunn and Martin Felsen, by the following student: Federico Diaz De Leon. See http://www.sprawlcity.us/ for more information about this course. Further modification and documentation was performed by members of the Center for Connected Learning and Computer-Based Modeling before releasing it as an Urban Suite model. The Urban Suite models were developed as part of the Procedural Modeling of Cities project, under the sponsorship of NSF ITR award 0326542, Electronic Arts & Maxis. Please see the project web site ( http://ccl.northwestern.edu/cities/ ) for more information.

verification.evidenceSummary: Urban land-cover change threatens biodiversity and affects ecosystem productivity through loss of habitat, biomass, and carbon storage. However, despite projections that world urban populations will increase to nearly 5 billion by 2030, little is known about future locations, magnitudes, and rates of urban expansion. Here we develop spatially explicit probabilistic forecasts of global urban land-cover change and explore the direct impacts on biodiversity hotspots and tropical carbon biomass. If current trends in population density continue and all areas with high probabilities of urban expansion undergo change, then by 2030, urban land cover will increase by 1.2 million km 2 , nearly tripling the global urban land area circa 2000.
